title: The Sale Happens in December. The Cost of Taking It Back Lands in February.
excerpt: Christmas trading looks like the year's best month on the profit and loss. For gift-driven retailers and online sellers, a meaningful share of that margin reverses in January and February, and few owners price for it.
content:
November and December carry more weight on the profit and loss than any other two months of the year for a gift-driven retailer, online store or hospitality venue. The revenue line climbs, the margin line climbs with it, and by the time the shop closes for the holidays the numbers on the screen look like the best quarter the business has had all year.

What those numbers do not yet show is how much of that December margin is coming back. A meaningful share of gift season sales do not stay sold. Wrong sizes, duplicate presents, a gift that was never quite right for the person who received it, all of it lands as a return or an exchange in the weeks after Christmas, clustering heavily through January and running into February.

None of this is a flaw in how the business traded in December. It is simply what gift buying does every single year, whether the business tracks it or not. The part worth catching now, before the Christmas rush is locked in, is that the margin booked at the point of sale is not the margin the business actually keeps once the return season runs its course.

What a Returned Sale Actually Costs

The refund itself is only the headline cost. Most payment processors keep their transaction fee even when a sale is reversed, so the business pays to receive the money and, in effect, pays again to give it back. Freight adds a second layer for anything sold online, covering the cost of the original delivery and, where return postage is covered by the seller, the cost of getting the item back as well. Someone then has to inspect it, repackage it and decide whether it can go back on the shelf as new stock or whether it is now being sold on the clearance rack at a markdown.

On a $120 jumper sold at a 50 percent gross margin, the $60 of gross profit the sale appeared to generate in December can be mostly gone by February once the non-refundable processing fee, the return freight and the clearance price it eventually resells at are all counted. Add the labour time spent processing the return rather than serving the next customer, and a sale that looked healthy in December can be close to break even, or worse, by the time it is fully wound back.

Why December's Margin Isn't February's Margin

The pattern we see across owner-led retail and e-commerce businesses is that monthly margin reporting tells a story in two instalments, and most owners only read the first one. December's management accounts show the sale, the revenue and the margin it appears to carry. The reversal, when it comes, lands in a different month's figures entirely, often after the owner has already mentally closed the book on Christmas trading and moved on to planning the new year. By the time the return cost shows up, it reads as a disappointing January or February rather than what it actually is, which is the back half of December's result arriving late.

The cash flow version of the same gap is just as real. Money that left the bank account as a refund or a replacement shipment in January was money the business had already counted as banked in December, and a business running tight on cash flow discipline through the new year can find a chunk of that discipline undone by refunds nobody planned the cash for.

Pricing and Provisioning for the Return Rate Already Coming

Most businesses that sell gifts already hold the data to answer this properly. Last year's return rate, by category and by sale channel, is sitting in the point of sale or e-commerce platform right now. Applying that rate to this year's Christmas sales forecast turns the return cost from a surprise into a line item, built into the margin forecast before the first gift is wrapped rather than discovered after the clearance rack is full.

Where the return policy itself can carry some of the weight, offering store credit alongside a cash refund, for example, keeps more of the value inside the business and avoids reversing the processing fee a second time, without making the policy noticeably less generous to the customer.

Working out where the margin on Christmas trading is genuinely holding and where it is quietly being handed back in February is exactly the kind of line-by-line question a Cost and Margin Deep Dive is built to answer, product by product and channel by channel rather than as one blended number for the whole gift season. Retailers and hospitality operators along the Gold Coast gearing up for the Christmas rush would do well to build the return provision into this year's forecast before the first sale rings through, rather than finding the answer in next year's February numbers. For businesses wanting a full picture of how trading peaks and troughs move through the year's margin, that is the kind of pattern a fractional CFO keeps an eye on well beyond any single season.

faqs.q: How much does a returned online order really cost a small retailer?
faqs.a: A refund rarely reverses only the sale price. Payment processing fees are often non-refundable even when a transaction is reversed, freight is usually paid twice if the seller covers return postage, and someone has to inspect, repackage and often remark down the item before it can be resold. Added together, the real cost of a return is usually well above the gross profit the original sale appeared to generate.

faqs.q: Why do product returns spike in January for Australian retailers?
faqs.a: Gift buying creates a predictable pattern every year. Wrong sizes, duplicate presents and gifts that simply were not quite right for the person who received them all surface once Christmas is over, and the exchanges and refunds that follow cluster heavily through January and into February. It happens regardless of how well a business traded through December, which is why it is worth planning for rather than treating as a surprise.

faqs.q: Should a business budget for Christmas returns before the sales season starts?
faqs.a: Yes, and the business already holds the data to do it properly. Last year's return rate by category and sale channel is sitting in the point of sale or e-commerce platform, and applying it to this year's forecast turns the return cost into a planned line item rather than a shock. Treating it as part of cash flow discipline through December and January keeps the new year's numbers from looking worse than the trading actually was.

faqs.q: Does offering store credit instead of a refund reduce the cost of a return?
faqs.a: It can. A refund reverses the sale in full, including handing back the processing fee the business already paid to receive the money and rarely gets back. Store credit keeps more of that value inside the business, often avoids reversing the processing fee a second time, and tends to bring the customer back for a future purchase, all without making the return policy noticeably less generous from the customer's side.

faqs.q: How does a Cost and Margin Deep Dive help with return related margin loss?
faqs.a: A Cost and Margin Deep Dive reviews cost structure and margin line by line rather than as one blended number for the whole gift season, which is exactly where return related costs tend to hide. It shows which products or channels are genuinely profitable once returns, freight and processing fees are counted, and which only look profitable until the return season runs its course.

faqs.q: Is the return rate for online sales usually higher than in-store purchases?
faqs.a: In our experience across owner-led retail and e-commerce businesses, online sales typically carry a higher return rate than in-store purchases, largely because the customer cannot try the item before buying and sizing or fit mismatches only become obvious once the parcel arrives. The gap tends to widen further during the gifting season, when the person buying the item is often not the person who ends up keeping it.

faqs.q: How does a fractional CFO help model the true margin of Christmas trading?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO brings the discipline of tracking how trading peaks like Christmas actually move through the full year's margin, not just the month the sale was made. That means building the expected return cost into the Christmas forecast from the outset, rather than discovering it as an unexplained dip in January or February once the season has already passed.
